name: wla-dx
why: Multi-platform retro CPU crossassembler, an old-school door into 8-bit console programming.

brief.what_it_is: WLA DX is a multi-platform cross-assembler package written in ANSI C. Its wla-ARCH programs assemble assembly source files into object or library files, and wlalink links those objects together. It covers many CPUs, including Z80, GB-Z80, 6502, 65816, 68000, 6809, 8080, HuC6280, SH-2, SPC700 and SuperFX. The package is not tied to one console, since you define your own memory map, which is shared across all object and library files. The Homebrew executables include wla-6502, wla-65816, wla-z80, wla-gb, wlab and wlalink, among others.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents WLA DX as 'Yet Another ANSI C' cross-assembler package. Its stated design point is that it isn't bound to one system such as the NES or C64; instead you define the memory map yourself.
brief.how_it_works: Each wla-ARCH assembler turns a source file into an object or library file. wlalink then combines those objects using the memory map you define. The README does not go into more detail on the internals. The docs index lists sections on linking, compiling object and library files, and an architectural overview, but I did not fetch those pages.

commands_seen.cmd: git clone https://github.com/vhelin/wla-dx # Clone the repository
commands_seen.context: README compile step 1: clones the source repository.
README compile step 2: enters the cloned source directory.

commands_seen.cmd: mkdir build && cd build # Create building directory
commands_seen.context: README compile step 3: creates and enters an out-of-tree build directory.
README compile step 4: generates the build system from the parent source directory. Optionally add -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=prefix to set the install location.
README compile step 5: builds the tools in Release configuration.
README compile step 6: installs the built tools. Optional; without it the binaries stay in the binaries folder.

brief.install_notes: Building from source needs CMake at least v2.8.12 and an ANSI C compiler. Sphinx is optional (min v1.2.0, v1.6.0 recommended) and is only needed to generate the docs. The README points to an INSTALL file for more detail, which I did not fetch. If you skip the install step, the binaries are in the binaries folder, and compiled docs are in its doc subfolder. Homebrew installs the executables directly, so the CMake steps are for building from source.
brief.standout: The memory map is user-defined rather than built into a console target, so one toolchain covers many CPU families. The CI matrix is also broad, with Linux sanitizers (ASan, UBSan, MSan), MSVC, Clang, GCC on macOS and Linux, and even Windows XP 32-bit.
brief.status: Maintained, with moderate confidence. The README has live Azure Pipelines badges across eight build configurations, and the docs are titled wla-dx 10.8a. I did not see a last-release or last-commit date, so I cannot confirm the release cadence.
brief.caveats: The license is GPL-2.0-or-later, which matters for embedding in proprietary projects. Building from source needs CMake and a C compiler, and the docs build needs Sphinx. The README alone does not show a getting-started example, so new users are sent to the external documentation. The Homebrew entry has no caveats of its own.
